say.text: Across every age group, which abdominal surgical emergency is the commonest?
Yes. Acute appendicitis is the commonest surgical cause of the acute abdomen, in every age group.
It stays the commonest non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy as well.
Cholecystitis is a real surgical emergency, and gallstones are common, so it feels like a safe pick.
Compare how often each condition needs surgery across all ages before you choose.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the ranking: it is set by frequency, not by how dramatic a disease looks.

say.text: Cholecystitis is common, but acute appendicitis is the commonest surgical cause of the acute abdomen.
So the list is headed by appendicitis.
Obstruction is dramatic on the wards, so it comes to mind quickly.
Ask which single condition the surgeon meets most often across all ages.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note this: the commonest surgical emergency is set by frequency, and that is appendicitis.

say.text: Intestinal obstruction is serious and needs surgery, but it is not the commonest surgical emergency of the abdomen.
Acute appendicitis is the commonest, so it heads the list in any age group.
Think about frequency, not drama: which condition does a surgeon see most often across every age group?
A 19-year-old describes the first hours of his pain. Which account fits classic appendicitis?

choices.label: Right iliac fossa pain from the start, moving to the umbilicus
Central colicky pain that later moves to the right iliac fossa
Repeated vomiting first, and central pain only later

say.text: Yes. Early pain is visceral, felt around the umbilicus, and shifts to the right iliac fossa once the parietal peritoneum is involved.
The classic order of symptoms is pain, then vomiting, then fever.
The right iliac fossa is where the pain is felt most sharply, so it looks like the starting point.
Ask where the pain is first sensed, and which part of the appendix is inflamed first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the start of the pain: it begins where the visceral nerves enter, and only later localises.

say.text: Early distension stimulates visceral afferents entering at T10, so the pain is first felt around the umbilicus.
Only when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum does the pain localise to the right iliac fossa. The shift runs from umbilicus to iliac fossa, not the reverse.
Vomiting is common and easy to recall, so putting it first feels natural.
Ask what the classic order of the three symptoms is, and which one starts the story.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember the order: vomiting before pain points away from appendicitis.

say.text: The classic sequence is pain, then vomiting, then fever. Anorexia is almost constant, and nausea and vomiting follow the onset of pain.
So vomiting before pain argues against appendicitis, and you should look for another cause.
Start with the mechanism: what sets off the pain, and which symptom follows it in the classic order?
The surgeon suspects a pelvic appendix and wants the manoeuvre that tests for it. Which one?

choices.label: Extension of the right hip, patient on the left side
Internal rotation of the flexed right hip
Pressure applied over the left iliac fossa

say.text: Yes. Internal rotation of the flexed hip stretches obturator internus, so pain suggests the appendix lies in the pelvis against it.
Both hip manoeuvres test the right side, so they feel interchangeable.
Ask which movement stretches the muscle that a pelvic appendix touches.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link each hip test to its muscle: the psoas for extension, the obturator for internal rotation.

say.text: Extension of the right hip is the psoas sign, which suggests a retrocaecal appendix lying on the psoas.
Internal rotation of the flexed hip is the obturator sign, which suggests a pelvic appendix in contact with obturator internus.
Pressure on one side is an easy test to remember, so it comes to mind for right-sided pain.
Ask what the left-sided pressure is meant to show, and whether the hip is needed here.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the pressure test from the hip tests: Rovsing's sign uses no hip movement.

say.text: Rovsing's sign is pressure in the left iliac fossa causing pain in the right iliac fossa.
It does not localise the appendix to the pelvis. The pelvic position is tested by the obturator manoeuvre.
A pelvic appendix lies against one muscle. Ask which movement stretches that muscle.
A young man has loin pain on hip extension and little anterior tenderness. Which pairing of sign and appendix position fits?

choices.label: Psoas sign with a pelvic appendix
Psoas sign with a retrocaecal appendix
Obturator sign with a retrocaecal appendix

say.text: Yes. Extension of the hip tests the psoas, which lies against a retrocaecal appendix, the most common position.
Both signs are common in exams, so the pelvic position feels like a neighbour of the psoas sign.
Ask where the appendix lies for each sign, rather than which sign is more common.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link each sign to its own position before you pair them.

say.text: The psoas sign suggests a retrocaecal appendix lying on the psoas muscle.
A pelvic appendix is the one that gives the obturator sign, so this pairing mixes the two positions.
The obturator and psoas tests come as a pair, so one may get attached to the position it does not belong to.
Ask which position the obturator sign is linked to, and then check the pairing.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the pair: the obturator sign goes with the pelvic appendix.

say.text: The obturator sign suggests a pelvic appendix in contact with obturator internus.
A retrocaecal appendix is the one that gives the psoas sign. Psoas with retrocaecal is the right pair.
Work out which muscle each sign tests, then ask which appendix position sits against that muscle.
A 26-year-old has anorexia, vomiting, tenderness in the right iliac fossa, a temperature of 38.2 C, and a left shift. What is the Alvarado total?

choices.label: 8, with fever scored as two points
6, with fever and left shift one point each
7, with left shift scored as two points

say.text: Yes. Only tenderness in the right iliac fossa and leucocytosis score two points; every other item scores one.
Fever feels like a strong sign, so it is natural to give it heavy weight.
Check how many items carry two points, and which ones they are.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the two-point items: fever is not one of them.

say.text: Only tenderness in the right iliac fossa and leucocytosis score two points. A raised temperature scores one.
The total for this patient is 6, not 8.
Left shift is a laboratory sign that feels significant, so it attracts extra weight in the mind.
Check the weight of each item before you add.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the weights item by item before you add.

say.text: A shift to the left scores one point. Migration and rebound also score one, and only the RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score two.
So the total is 6, not 7.
Add the items one at a time, and remember that only two items score two points.
An adult man has right iliac fossa pain for two days. Graded-compression ultrasound does not show the appendix. What do you conclude?

choices.label: A normal ultrasound rules out appendicitis here
Repeat the ultrasound, as it is the most accurate test
Non-visualisation does not exclude it; contrast CT is next

say.text: Yes. A missing appendix on ultrasound does not exclude disease in an adult; contrast CT abdomen is the most accurate test here.
It also shows complications such as an abscess, perforation or an appendicolith.
A normal scan feels reassuring, and ultrasound is the first test in many patients.
Ask what a missing appendix on a scan actually means in an adult.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note this: a view that is not obtained is not a normal appendix.

say.text: A missing appendix on ultrasound is not a normal appendix. Contrast CT has the highest sensitivity and specificity in adults.
So a negative ultrasound in an adult needs CT before the patient is discharged or observed.
Ultrasound is the usual first test, and older exam keys favoured it, so it sounds like the answer.
Check the age group the stem describes before you choose the test.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the old key from the adult rule.

say.text: PYQs have expected ultrasound as the investigation of choice for appendicitis in general.
In adults, current practice uses contrast CT as the most accurate test. Ultrasound comes first in children and pregnancy.
Separate two questions: does a missing appendix on the scan mean it is normal, and which test is most accurate in an adult?
A woman at 26 weeks of pregnancy has right iliac fossa pain. Which imaging pathway is correct?

choices.label: MRI first, to avoid radiation to the fetus
Ultrasound first, then MRI without gadolinium if inconclusive
Contrast CT first, as it is the fastest test

say.text: Yes. In pregnancy, graded-compression ultrasound is the first test; MRI without gadolinium follows when ultrasound is inconclusive.
MRI carries no radiation, so it feels like the safest first step in pregnancy.
Ask what the first test in pregnancy is, and when MRI is used.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the order: MRI is a second-line test in pregnancy, after ultrasound.

say.text: Ultrasound is the initial test in pregnancy. MRI without gadolinium follows when ultrasound is inconclusive.
Choosing MRI first skips the test that comes first in this group.
CT is the most accurate test in adults and fast, so it feels like a first step in any patient.
Ask which patient group the CT first-choice applies to.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that the CT first-choice is an adult rule, not a pregnancy rule.

say.text: Contrast CT is the most accurate test in adults. It is not the first test in children or in pregnant women.
In pregnancy, ultrasound comes first, and MRI follows if it is inconclusive.
Think about which test comes first in this patient group, before any second-line test.
A 24-year-old woman has right iliac fossa pain and a late period. What comes before imaging or theatre?

choices.label: Go to theatre now, and test later
Urine or serum beta-hCG now, before any scan
Treat it as appendicitis, since RIF pain means it

say.text: Yes. A beta-hCG test in every woman of reproductive age excludes ectopic pregnancy before imaging or surgery.
Theatre feels urgent, and a blood test seems like a delay.
Ask what must be excluded before you commit to imaging or an operation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember the pregnancy test is a fast step that comes before both scan and theatre.

say.text: Ectopic pregnancy is one of the conditions that mimic appendicitis in women, so the test must come first.
The test takes minutes, so there is no reason to skip it, even for a quick operation.
RIF pain is the classic story for appendicitis, so the diagnosis can feel settled.
Ask which other conditions cause RIF pain in a woman of this age.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that RIF pain has several causes in women, and the site alone does not settle the diagnosis.

say.text: RIF pain does not always mean appendicitis. In women, ectopic pregnancy, a ruptured ovarian cyst and pelvic inflammatory disease also cause it.
A ruptured Graafian follicle, mittelschmerz, can mimic it too. Check the pregnancy test and the history before you operate.
Ask what must be excluded first in a woman of reproductive age, before any scan or operation.
A motivated 34-year-old man has CT-proven uncomplicated appendicitis with no appendicolith. Which statement is right?

choices.label: Appendicectomy is the only treatment for him
Antibiotics-first is an accepted option for him
Antibiotics-first, even with a localised perforation

say.text: Yes. Antibiotics-first is accepted for selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated appendicitis, though some need surgery later for recurrence.
Surgery was the only answer in older teaching, so it feels like the safe default.
Ask whether the stem limits the choice to CT-proven uncomplicated disease.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that the only-treatment key is an older exam answer that practice has moved past.

say.text: PYQs have expected appendicectomy as the only treatment. Current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected CT-proven uncomplicated cases.
Recurrence is the main price, so some of these patients still need an appendicectomy later.
Antibiotics are a sound option in the right patient, so the choice can feel general.
Check whether the disease is complicated before you apply the option.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember that antibiotics-first is limited to uncomplicated disease.

say.text: Antibiotics-first is limited to CT-proven uncomplicated disease. An appendicolith predicts failure of antibiotics.
A localised collection needs image-guided drainage or surgery, not antibiotics alone.
Ask which features on the scan would make antibiotics alone less safe for this man.
A 55-year-old man's appendicular mass has resolved on conservative treatment. What is the next step?

choices.label: Routine interval appendicectomy at 6-8 weeks for all
Colonoscopy or CT to exclude cancer, then selective surgery
Immediate appendicectomy while the mass settles

say.text: Yes. In an older patient, colonoscopy or CT first excludes caecal carcinoma, and interval surgery is then selective.
The 6-8 week interval is standard teaching, so routine surgery feels like a required step.
Ask whether that rule still applies to every patient, and what an older patient needs first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that the interval rule is now selective, and older patients need the tumour excluded.

say.text: PYQs have expected interval appendicectomy at 6-8 weeks after a mass. Current practice makes it selective.
In older patients, colonoscopy or CT excludes caecal carcinoma before any interval surgery.
A mass is an inflamed appendix, and early removal feels like the fix.
Ask what the regimen is for a mass, and what this mass is doing on treatment.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that a mass which settles on the regimen does not need immediate surgery.

say.text: An appendicular mass is first managed by the Ochsner-Sherren regimen: nil by mouth, fluids, antibiotics and charting.
Here the mass has resolved on treatment, so immediate surgery is not the next step.
A 28-year-old has a right groin bulge and numbness after open appendicectomy through a gridiron incision. Which complication fits?

choices.label: Right inguinal hernia from iliohypogastric nerve injury
Right inguinal hernia from ilioinguinal nerve injury

say.text: Yes. A gridiron incision can injure the ilioinguinal nerve, and that injury gives the right inguinal hernia.
Before you finish, the appendix tumour key: the commonest tumour is the carcinoid, usually at the tip.
Under 2 cm at the tip, appendicectomy alone is usually curative. Over 2 cm, or at the base, needs right hemicolectomy.
Pylephlebitis is a serious complication, so it comes to mind after any abdominal operation.
Ask what the groin bulge and numbness point to at the incision.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that pylephlebitis comes from the disease, not from this incision.

say.text: Pylephlebitis is septic thrombosis of the portal venous system from the disease itself, with liver abscesses.
The groin signs point to the nerve at the gridiron incision, not to the portal veins.
The iliohypogastric nerve lies close to the ilioinguinal nerve, so the two are easy to mix.
Ask which nerve is injured by a gridiron incision, and gives the hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so name the nerve at risk with this incision.

say.text: A gridiron incision puts the ilioinguinal nerve at risk, and its injury gives a right inguinal hernia.
The neighbouring nerve is not the one named for this incision.
